answer: SELECT T3.forename ,  T3.surname FROM races AS T1 JOIN results AS T2 ON T1.raceid = T2.raceid JOIN drivers AS T3 ON T2.driverid = T3.driverid WHERE T1.name = "Australian Grand Prix" EXCEPT SELECT T3.forename ,  T3.surname FROM races AS T1 JOIN results AS T2 ON T1.raceid = T2.raceid JOIN drivers AS T3 ON T2.driverid = T3.driverid WHERE T1.name = "Chinese Grand Prix"

prefix_hints.hint_1: Build the Australian race participation set by joining races to results and then to driver details through their shared identifiers: `FROM races AS T1 JOIN results AS T2 ON T1.raceid = T2.raceid JOIN drivers AS T3 ON T2.driverid = T3.driverid`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Restrict the first joined set to participation records from the Australian Grand Prix: `WHERE T1.name = "Australian Grand Prix"`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Project each participating driver's first and last names for the first result set: `SELECT T3.forename ,  T3.surname`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Construct the second result set containing the names of drivers who participated in the Chinese Grand Prix: `SELECT T3.forename ,  T3.surname FROM races AS T1 JOIN results AS T2 ON T1.raceid = T2.raceid JOIN drivers AS T3 ON T2.driverid = T3.driverid WHERE T1.name = "Chinese Grand Prix"`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Place the set-difference operator between the Australian and Chinese participation queries so that names present in the Chinese set are removed from the Australian set: `EXCEPT`.

answer: SELECT DISTINCT T1.forename FROM drivers AS T1 JOIN driverstandings AS T2 ON T1.driverid = T2.driverid WHERE T2.position = 1 AND T2.wins = 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the `drivers` table because it contains the requested driver forenames: `FROM drivers AS T1`.

prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the standing records to drivers who held first position: `WHERE T2.position = 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Add the requirement that the first-position standing record reports one win: `AND T2.wins = 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the drivers’ forenames and use `DISTINCT` so each qualifying forename appears once: `SELECT DISTINCT T1.forename`.

Question:
What are the line 1 of addresses shared by some students and some teachers?
answer: SELECT T1.line_1 FROM Addresses AS T1 JOIN Students AS T2 ON T1.address_id  =  T2.address_id INTERSECT SELECT T1.line_1 FROM Addresses AS T1 JOIN Teachers AS T2 ON T1.address_id  =  T2.address_id

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start with `Addresses` and connect each address to students through the shared `address_id`: `FROM Addresses AS T1 JOIN Students AS T2 ON T1.address_id = T2.address_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Project the first address line from the student-address rows: `SELECT T1.line_1`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Build the corresponding address-to-teacher relationship using the same address key: `FROM Addresses AS T1 JOIN Teachers AS T2 ON T1.address_id = T2.address_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Project the first address line from the teacher-address rows as the second result set: `SELECT T1.line_1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Place the set intersection operator between the student-address query and the teacher-address query so only address lines appearing in both sets remain: `INTERSECT`.

prefix_hints.hint_2: Keep only assets having exactly two associated part rows by applying the aggregate condition: `HAVING count(*) = 2`.

Question:
What are the course codes for every class that the student with the last name Smithson took?
answer: SELECT T1.crs_code FROM CLASS AS T1 JOIN enroll AS T2 ON T1.class_code  =  T2.class_code JOIN student AS T3 ON T3.stu_num  =  T2.stu_num WHERE T3.stu_lname  =  'Smithson'

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the class records because each class directly contains the requested course code: `FROM CLASS AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Connect each class to its enrollment records using the shared class code: `JOIN enroll AS T2 ON T1.class_code = T2.class_code`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Link each enrollment to the corresponding student through the student number: `JOIN student AS T3 ON T3.stu_num = T2.stu_num`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Restrict the joined records to the student whose last name is Smithson: `WHERE T3.stu_lname = 'Smithson'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the course code from each qualifying class in the SELECT clause: `SELECT T1.crs_code`.

Question:
How many professors who are from either Accounting or Biology department?
answer: SELECT count(*) FROM professor AS T1 JOIN department AS T2 ON T1.dept_code  =  T2.dept_code WHERE T2.dept_name  =  'Accounting' OR T2.dept_name  =  'Biology'

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the table containing one record for each professor and assign it the alias used by the query: `FROM professor AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each professor to the corresponding department through their shared department code: `JOIN department AS T2 ON T1.dept_code = T2.dept_code`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Use the department name column to identify professors belonging to Accounting: `T2.dept_name = 'Accounting'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Include Biology as the alternative qualifying department by combining both name conditions with OR: `WHERE T2.dept_name = 'Accounting' OR T2.dept_name = 'Biology'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return the number of professor rows that remain after the join and department filter using the aggregate projection: `SELECT count(*)`.

What are the manager's first name, last name and id who won the most manager award?
answer: SELECT T1.name_first ,  T1.name_last ,  T2.player_id FROM player AS T1 JOIN manager_award AS T2 ON T1.player_id  =  T2.player_id GROUP BY T2.player_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1;

prefix_hints.hint_4: Keep only the top-ranked manager, who has won the most awards: `LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the top manager’s first name, last name, and player identifier at the beginning of the assembled query: `SELECT T1.name_first, T1.name_last, T2.player_id`.

What is the highest salary among each team? List the team name, id and maximum salary.
answer: SELECT T1.name ,  T1.team_id ,  max(T2.salary) FROM team AS T1 JOIN salary AS T2 ON T1.team_id  =  T2.team_id GROUP BY T1.team_id;

prefix_hints.hint_3: Calculate the highest salary within each resulting team group using the aggregate expression: `max(T2.salary)`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Create one aggregate result per team identifier so the maximum is computed separately for each team: `GROUP BY T1.team_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the team name, team ID, and calculated maximum salary in the SELECT clause: `SELECT T1.name, T1.team_id, max(T2.salary)`.

Question:
What are the name and id of the team offering the lowest average salary?
answer: SELECT T1.name ,  T1.team_id FROM team AS T1 JOIN salary AS T2 ON T1.team_id = T2.team_id GROUP BY T1.team_id ORDER BY avg(T2.salary) ASC LIMIT 1;

prefix_hints.hint_1: Link each team record to its salary records through the shared team identifier: `FROM team AS T1 JOIN salary AS T2 ON T1.team_id = T2.team_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Group the joined salary rows by team so that an average can be calculated for each team: `GROUP BY T1.team_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Use the salary values within each team group to calculate its average salary: `avg(T2.salary)`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Sort teams from the lowest average salary to the highest: `ORDER BY avg(T2.salary) ASC`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the team name and identifier, then retain only the first team in the ascending ranking: `SELECT T1.name ,  T1.team_id` and `LIMIT 1`.

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start the first result set by selecting players’ first and last names from `player` alongside award records: `SELECT T1.name_first , T1.name_last FROM player AS T1 JOIN player_award AS T2`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Restrict the first result set to award records from 1960: `WHERE T2.year = 1960`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Build the second result set with the same player-name projection and award-table aliases: `SELECT T1.name_first , T1.name_last FROM player AS T1 JOIN player_award AS T2`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Restrict this second result set to award records from 1961: `WHERE T2.year = 1961`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Place the set operator between the 1960 and 1961 SELECT statements so that only names occurring in both results remain: `... WHERE T2.year = 1960 INTERSECT SELECT ... WHERE T2.year = 1961`.

Question:
List the maximum scores of the team Boston Red Stockings when the team won in postseason?
answer: SELECT max(T1.wins) FROM postseason AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_winner  =  T2.team_id_br WHERE T2.name  =  'Boston Red Stockings';

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the postseason results because each winning team and its number of wins are recorded there: `FROM postseason AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join each postseason winner to the corresponding team record using the winner’s team ID and the team’s Baseball-Reference ID: `JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_winner = T2.team_id_br`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined records to the team named Boston Red Stockings: `WHERE T2.name = 'Boston Red Stockings'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Apply the maximum aggregate to the postseason wins column to find the team’s highest winning score: `max(T1.wins)`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Use the maximum-wins expression as the query’s projection, placing it before the joined tables and team-name filter: `SELECT max(T1.wins)`.

Question:
What are the name and id of the team with the most victories in 2008 postseason?
answer: SELECT T2.name ,  T1.team_id_winner FROM postseason AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_winner  =  T2.team_id_br WHERE T1.year  =  2008 GROUP BY T1.team_id_winner ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1;

prefix_hints.hint_1: Link each postseason winner record to its team details by matching the winner identifier to the team’s Baseball-Reference identifier: `FROM postseason AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_winner = T2.team_id_br`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Restrict the postseason records to the requested 2008 season: `WHERE T1.year = 2008`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the matching postseason rows by winning team so each team’s victories can be counted: `GROUP BY T1.team_id_winner`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank teams by their number of winning postseason records and retain the top team: `ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the selected team’s name and winning-team identifier in the result: `SELECT T2.name, T1.team_id_winner`.

Find the name and id of the team that won the most times in 2008 postseason.
answer: SELECT T2.name ,  T1.team_id_winner FROM postseason AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_winner  =  T2.team_id_br WHERE T1.year  =  2008 GROUP BY T1.team_id_winner ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1;

prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the matched postseason rows by winning team so each team's number of wins can be counted: `GROUP BY T1.team_id_winner`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank the teams by their postseason win count in descending order and keep only the top team: `ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the winning team's name from the team table together with its postseason winner ID: `SELECT T2.name, T1.team_id_winner`.

Question:
What is the number of wins the team Boston Red Stockings got in the postseasons each year in history?
answer: SELECT count(*) ,  T1.year FROM postseason AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_winner  =  T2.team_id_br WHERE T2.name  =  'Boston Red Stockings' GROUP BY T1.year

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start with postseason records because each row identifies a winning team and the year of that postseason: `FROM postseason AS T1`.

prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined records to the team named Boston Red Stockings: `WHERE T2.name = 'Boston Red Stockings'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Create one result group for each postseason year so the winning records can be counted annually: `GROUP BY T1.year`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the number of matching postseason wins and the corresponding year for each group: `SELECT count(*), T1.year`.

Question:
How many times in total did the team Boston Red Stockings participate in postseason games?
answer: SELECT count(*) FROM ( SELECT * FROM postseason AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_winner  =  T2.team_id_br WHERE T2.name  =  'Boston Red Stockings' UNION SELECT * FROM postseason AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_loser  =  T2.team_id_br WHERE T2.name  =  'Boston Red Stockings' );

prefix_hints.hint_1: Build the first postseason branch by matching each winning team identifier to the team's Baseball-Reference identifier: `FROM postseason AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_winner = T2.team_id_br`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Restrict the winning-team branch to Boston Red Stockings records and retain each matching row for the later set operation: `SELECT * FROM postseason AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_winner = T2.team_id_br WHERE T2.name = 'Boston Red Stockings'`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Build the second branch by matching the postseason losing-team identifier to the same team identifier column: `FROM postseason AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_loser = T2.team_id_br`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Filter the losing-team branch to Boston Red Stockings and combine it with the winning-team branch using a set union: `UNION SELECT * FROM postseason AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_loser = T2.team_id_br WHERE T2.name = 'Boston Red Stockings'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Wrap the union of the winning and losing branches as a derived table, then count all rows representing postseason participation: `SELECT count(*) FROM ( ... )`.

prefix_hints.hint_2: Join each salary record to the team information using the salary team identifier and the team's Baseball-Reference identifier: `JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id = T2.team_id_br`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined records to the team named Boston Red Stockings: `WHERE T2.name = 'Boston Red Stockings'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Add the salary-year condition so that only payments made in 2010 are included: `AND T1.year = 2010`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Calculate the total of all qualifying salary amounts with the aggregate projection: `SELECT sum(T1.salary)`.

Question:
What is the total salary expenses of team Boston Red Stockings in 2010?
answer: SELECT sum(T1.salary) FROM salary AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id  =  T2.team_id_br WHERE T2.name  = 'Boston Red Stockings' AND T1.year  =  2010

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the salary records because they contain the individual salary amounts to be totaled: `FROM salary AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join each salary record to its team using the salary table’s team identifier and the team table’s Baseball-Reference identifier: `JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id = T2.team_id_br`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined records to the team named Boston Red Stockings: `WHERE T2.name = 'Boston Red Stockings'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Further restrict the salary records to the requested year, 2010: `AND T1.year = 2010`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Calculate the team’s total salary expense by summing all qualifying salary values in the projection: `SELECT sum(T1.salary)`.

Question:
Which team had the least number of attendances in home games in 1980?
answer: SELECT T2.name FROM home_game AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id = T2.team_id_br WHERE T1.year = 1980 ORDER BY T1.attendance ASC LIMIT 1;

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start with the home-game records, which contain both the season and attendance figures: `FROM home_game AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join each home-game record to its team so the team name can be retrieved, using the home-game team ID and the team’s Baseball-Reference ID: `JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id = T2.team_id_br`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the home-game records to the requested 1980 season: `WHERE T1.year = 1980`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Sort attendance from lowest to highest and keep only the first record, which identifies the least-attended team: `ORDER BY T1.attendance ASC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the name of the team associated with that minimum-attendance record by placing this clause at the beginning: `SELECT T2.name`.

prefix_hints.hint_5: Retain groups with at least two qualifying mailshots and project their customer names using these clauses: `HAVING count(*) >= 2` and `SELECT T2.customer_name`.

prefix_hints.hint_3: Build the corresponding source for performer locations by joining addresses to performers on the same key: `FROM Addresses AS T1 JOIN Performers AS T2 ON T1.Address_ID = T2.Address_ID`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Project the cities containing performers to form the result set that must be removed: `SELECT T1.City_Town FROM Addresses AS T1 JOIN Performers AS T2 ON T1.Address_ID = T2.Address_ID`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Place the set-difference operator between the customer-city result and the performer-city result so only customer cities absent from the latter remain: `EXCEPT`.

Question:
